title: Biggest Number From One Digit Swap
statement:
You get a non-negative integer num. You may swap two of its digits at most once, or leave it alone. Return the largest number you can get.

Leading zeros cannot appear, since the result is never smaller than num.

examples.why: Move the 8 to the front by swapping it with the 3.
There are two 9s. Swapping the 1 with the last 9 gives 9913; using the first 9 gives only 9193.
Digits already fall from left to right, so every swap makes it smaller. Keep it.

hints: The leftmost digit you can improve matters more than anything to its right. Where should the swap happen?
Find the first position, from the left, that has a bigger digit somewhere after it.
Swap that position with the largest digit to its right, and if that digit appears several times, take its last occurrence.

explain.intuition:
A bigger digit further left beats any change further right, so walk from the left and stop at the first digit that has something larger after it. That is the one to replace. Replace it with the largest digit that appears later.

When the largest later digit appears several times, use its last copy. The digit you push back lands where that copy was, and the further right a smaller digit lands, the less it costs: 1993 becomes 9913, not 9193. Storing the last index of each digit 0–9 makes the whole thing one pass.
steps: Turn num into an array of digits.
Record last[d], the last index where digit d appears.
For each position i from the left, try digits d from 9 down to digits[i] + 1. If last[d] > i, swap positions i and last[d] and stop.
Turn the digits back into a number and return it.
pitfalls: Swapping with the first copy of the largest digit instead of the last one. 1993 would give 9193.
Swapping the largest digit with the very first digit even when the first digit is already the largest. 9973 must stay as it is, and the swap belongs at the first position that can be improved.
Swapping whenever a later digit is merely larger, instead of the largest later digit. 1293 must become 9213, not 2193.

complexity.time: O(d) where d is the number of digits (at most 9)

solutions.title: Try every pair
solutions.idea: Swap every pair of positions, read the number, keep the largest. With at most 9 digits this is only 36 swaps.

solutions.title: Last index of each digit
solutions.idea: Fix the first position that has a larger digit after it, swapping in the largest such digit at its last occurrence.

followups: Return the smallest number you can make with one swap, without creating a leading zero.
You may make up to k swaps. Does the greedy still work, and what does it cost?
